deck.headline: Lean community certifies AI-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof as correct after independent checks
deck.sub: Two days after Levent Alpöge released a 17-million-line machine-checked proof built with Claude, the people who maintain Lean say the statement and the proof are both right.
deck.summary: The Lean and Mathlib communities say Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, built with an internal Claude model, is correct. Dozens rebuilt it, two tools confirmed it proves exactly Mathlib's statement, and independent checkers accepted it. MIT's Andrew Sutherland reports all 175,187 modules compile; two of his checks were still running.
deck.whyItMatters: Machine-checked AI-assisted proofs are now trusted by the people who run the checker, within two days. Expect the same pattern (AI writes, a formal checker certifies) in software, smart contracts and risk models; the open question is understanding the new ideas, not whether they are right.
deck.checked: Joint statement opened on the Lean community blog; MIT verification page opened (module counts, axioms, byte-identical rebuild); The Decoder opened for context
deck.detailHtml:
The Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, published a joint statement on 21 Nov: "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct." The proof, released on 20 Nov as a Lean library of 17 million lines, depends only on Mathlib. Dozens of people rebuilt it and got the same proof export; the community isolated Mathlib's own statement of the hypothesis and two separate tools (comparator and con-leche) confirmed the library proves exactly that; and several proof checkers, including Lean's kernel and checkers written in other languages, accepted the exported proof. Two of them (con-leche, con-ron) come with a formal proof that they cannot accept a false proof. MIT's Andrew Sutherland, who ran his checks with Claude Code, reports all 175,187 modules compile, the five headline theorems use only the three standard axioms, and a sandboxed rebuild reproduced the 61.6GB export byte for byte; two checks were still running on 22 Nov. Metaculus forecasters had expected a proof around 2035.

On 20 Nov Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working with an internal Claude model, released a Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, the 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are distributed. On 21 Nov the communities that build Lean and its maths library certified it: the statement is Mathlib's own, the code compiles for everyone who tried, and independent checkers accept the proof. Mathematicians still have to understand the new ideas inside it.

deck.headline: OpenAI's chief scientist asks rival labs to agree shared limits on AI pretraining progress
deck.sub: Jakub Pachocki publishes OpenAI's internal perplexity curve and proposes a cross-lab cap until monitoring catches up.
deck.summary: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes that labs track pretraining perplexity as a shared measure and agree limits they will not cross until monitoring improves. OpenAI publishes its curve: GPT-4 at about 0.91, recent models below 0.8, and a 0.76 model producing breakthrough maths results. He warns of rapid AI-driven pretraining advances as soon as 2027. Altman backs it.
deck.whyItMatters: This is the first frontier lab to publish its own pretraining curve and ask for a cross-industry cap. Whether Anthropic, Google and xAI sign up decides if it becomes a standard regulators can point to, as Democrats prepare to make AI oversight a priority in the new Congress.
deck.checked: OpenAI's post opened (numbers and proposal quoted from it); Reuters copy on Yahoo opened for Altman's backing
deck.storyline: Storyline: how fast frontier AI is moving · day 27
deck.detailHtml: In a post titled Perplexity and Intelligence, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki argues that pretraining loss (perplexity) is the best single measure of how capable a model's base is, and publishes OpenAI's internal numbers: GPT-3.5 at ~0.99 log-perplexity, GPT-4 at ~0.91, and recent models below 0.8, where 'transformative capabilities' in cybersecurity and maths appeared. A model at ~0.76 'started producing groundbreaking results' on open maths problems. He expects more as models reach 0.68-0.7, warns AI could set off an 'avalanche' of pretraining advances as soon as 2027, and says alignment auditing will likely get worse. He proposes common limits, 'based on perplexity and other measurements', that developers commit not to cross until monitoring reaches a concrete milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. Reuters reports Sam Altman backs the proposal; no response yet from other labs.

deck.headline: OpenRouter drops three AI providers after researchers catch prompts and keys being stolen
deck.sub: Dragos seeded two million prompts with fake AWS keys; attackers used them within a day, and 'zero data retention' flags did not stop it.
deck.summary: Dragos seeded about two million prompts with fake AWS keys and found attackers inside three AI hosting providers, using stolen keys within hours, even on zero-data-retention requests. Marketplace resellers could also read prompts. OpenRouter has off-boarded three providers, pulled 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention and notified customers; it says its own systems were not breached.
deck.whyItMatters: A 'privacy' flag binds only the first hop. Banks routing prompts through model marketplaces should pin providers, keep credentials out of prompts and agent context, and treat any key that went through a third-party inference provider since July as exposed.
deck.checked: OpenRouter's announcement opened (three providers off-boarded, 125 endpoints, provider notices); Dragos research post opened (method and findings)
deck.storyline: Storyline: who can see your AI prompts · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Dragos (research led by HD Moore) sent about two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary AWS credentials to AI services from July to November. It found attackers inside three hosting providers, copying requests 'at the provider's front door'; in the largest case every request sent in late-October windows was stolen, a couple of hundred AWS keys were tested within hours and used for tens of thousands of API calls, including attempts to enable Bedrock models and add IAM users. Some stolen requests were flagged zero-data-retention. Separately, resellers on an inference marketplace could read and keep customer prompts using ordinary logging, and some providers sent prompts to Chinese companies against their stated policies. OpenRouter says no breach of its own systems, but it has off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility, notified affected customers and will run similar canary tests continuously. Together, Novita, Phala and Atlas Cloud have published notices.

deck.headline: California opens criminal angle on Nvidia's China chip sales as pressure to reinstate Huang grows
deck.summary: California's attorney general says his Nvidia probe covers possible criminal violations of state law over China chip sales and statements to investors, on top of the SEC accounting probe. Shopify's CEO called Nvidia's board 'knuckleheads' as a petition for Jensen Huang's return passed 100,000 signatures; the board refuses. Congressional hearings are set for 1-2 December.
deck.whyItMatters: A state criminal angle raises the stakes for Nvidia's executives and directors and for lenders with Nvidia exposure; the 1-2 Dec hearings and Nvidia's delayed 10-Q are the next dates.
deck.update: California's attorney general confirms a probe that includes possible criminal violations of state law over Nvidia's China chip sales and statements to investors; Shopify's Tobi Lütke calls Nvidia's board 'knuckleheads' as a petition for Huang's return passes 100,000 signatures; congressional hearings are set for 1-2 Dec
deck.detailHtml: Rob Bonta told Bloomberg the state is looking at 'prohibitions in California law, both civil and criminal, against misleading investors and the public', and at whether Nvidia or former CEO Jensen Huang gave false information about sales to China. The probe was prompted partly by Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive US intelligence suspects of spying; Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips. It runs alongside the SEC accounting investigation (now including Nvidia's 2025 switch from billing-address to headquarters-based geographic revenue reporting, which removed Singapore as a separate line) and a DOJ export-control inquiry. Shopify's Tobi Lütke used a 22 Nov podcast to call the directors 'knuckleheads'; a petition for Huang's return has passed 100,000 signatures, but the board, which named Colette Kress interim CEO, has refused. Congressional hearings on Nvidia's leadership are set for 1-2 Dec. The WSJ reports that Li Ming, a partner of Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, ran the network that moved chips to China (paywalled; not opened). Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53.

deck.headline: Kalshi faces New York hearing it says could shut its exchange nationwide
deck.summary: A New York judge hears the attorney general's bid to restrain Kalshi on Monday. Kalshi says the order would shut its exchange for every customer because it is based in New York; the AG says it would not. A federal judge rejected the CFTC's second emergency bid to stop the case on 20 Nov. New York seeks up to $36bn.
deck.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest test yet of whether states can police federally regulated event contracts; brokers and banks building prediction-market products (Coinbase plans its own in 2027) should watch the order's scope.
deck.storyline: Storyline: prediction markets and their rules · day 8
deck.detailHtml: New York's attorney general wants an order barring Kalshi from running what she calls unlicensed gambling 'within or from New York', restricting trading by under-21s and banning campus advertising. Kalshi's lawyers say that because the exchange is based in New York the order would force it to stop serving all clients and possibly liquidate every open position; the AG says she does not intend to shut its national business. The case was sent back to the New York County Supreme Court on 19 Nov, and on 20 Nov a federal judge in Manhattan rejected the CFTC's second emergency request to stop it. The suit, filed 31 Jul, seeks up to $36bn in restitution and penalties, more than Kalshi's reported $22bn valuation. This was held back on 21 Nov because the sources could not be opened.

deck.headline: South Korea's education minister resigns over AI cheating scandal around national exams
deck.summary: South Korea's education minister resigned after AI-assisted cheating fears upended the national university exam. The top scorer on the tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden camera and AI answers on a phone, prompting wifi blocks, doubled supervisors and rewards of at least $75,000 for reports. The exam itself passed without major incidents.
deck.whyItMatters: High-stakes testing, including professional certification such as banking and accounting exams, now has to assume a hidden camera and a frontier model; expect a move to supervised digital testing and oral checks.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI cheating in exams · day 3
deck.detailHtml: Choi Kyo-jin, 72, resigned saying he takes 'full responsibility' for failing to prepare, after a week in which the top scorer on Korea's national tax accountant exam admitted he photographed the questions with a concealed micro-camera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. Four days later 500,000-plus students sat the suneung under emergency rules: public wifi blocked near test sites, twice as many supervisors, pencils only, stickers over clothing buttons that could hide cameras, and a reward of at least $75,000 for reporting cheating. Choi had told parliament that 'due to my age' he was not confident cheaters could be caught. The Guardian and BBC report the exam passed without major incidents; Korean media say the ministry is extending its investigation to past suneung exams.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Guardian: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal · BBC: South Korea education minister resigns

deck.headline: COP31 climate talks end without a major deal after row over fossil fuels
deck.summary: COP31 in Turkey ended on Sunday without a major new climate deal after the longest UN climate talks ever. The final text never mentions fossil fuels; the EU, Pacific islands and others objected, and poorer countries got no clear adaptation money. Guterres said he was deeply disappointed; the BBC compares it to Copenhagen in 2009.
deck.whyItMatters: With no new multilateral push, climate policy shifts back to national rules and markets; for banks that means more weight on EU and UK disclosure rules and on physical-risk pricing, not on a global carbon pathway.
deck.detailHtml: Talks in Antalya were due to end on Friday but ran into Sunday, making this the longest UN climate conference on record. A draft presented early on Sunday did not contain the words 'fossil fuels', only a nod to the COP28 pledge to 'transition away' from them. The EU's negotiator, Irish minister Darragh O'Brien, said it went 'nowhere near' the ambition needed; Panama and the Marshall Islands also objected, and poorer countries complained of no clear money from richer nations for adaptation. António Guterres, at his last COP, blamed 'powerful fossil fuel interests'. In Australia, which hosts negotiations next year, the Liberals demanded energy minister Chris Bowen resign over the outcome. A storage alliance with CATL, BYD and ACWA was launched on the sidelines.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal

deck.headline: Democrats win biggest House majority since 1992, setting up a divided government
deck.summary: Democrats now hold at least 258 House seats after a North Carolina recount, their biggest majority since 1992, and the Senate is also Democratic. They plan a 100-day cost-of-living agenda, broad oversight of Trump and an early vote to ban lawmakers trading stocks. Expect hearings on AI chips, Nvidia, outages and data-centre power.
deck.whyItMatters: The incoming House controls appropriations and investigations; expect hearings on AI chip exports, Nvidia, the tech outages and data-centre power costs, and slower deregulation of banks and crypto.
deck.storyline: Storyline: who controls the US Congress · day 1
deck.detailHtml: With Chuck Hubbard's victory in North Carolina after a recount, Democrats hold at least 258 of 435 House seats to Republicans' at least 173, the most for the party since 1992 (258) and 2008 (257). The Senate is also Democratic, so President Trump faces a divided Congress from January. Democrats say they will pass a 100-day agenda on living costs and run extensive oversight; Hakeem Jeffries says a ban on lawmakers trading stocks will come 'very early'. AI is on the list: a Democratic lawmaker told The Hill the next Congress will focus on AI in healthcare, jobs and agriculture, and the Senate passed a data-centre permitting and grid-cost bill last week.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Guardian: House Democrats historic sweep · BBC: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992

deck.headline: Software billing firm Cleverbridge says hackers stole card numbers and CVV codes
deck.summary: Cleverbridge, which handles payments for software vendors such as Red Hat, Veeam and Parallels, says hackers copied payment card data from its platform. It detected the intrusion on 4 Nov and began notifying buyers on 20 Nov; notices list card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes. It has not said how many cards are affected.
deck.whyItMatters: Card issuers should expect fraud on cards used for software purchases since early November and consider reissuing; merchants of record are a concentrated target, and this one apparently held the security codes that should never be kept.
deck.detailHtml: Cleverbridge sells software and subscriptions on behalf of vendors such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony and Parallels. It says it spotted unauthorised activity on 4 Nov, took systems offline and brought them back the same day, but later found a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform. It began notifying affected buyers on 20 Nov; a notice seen by BleepingComputer lists card number, expiry date and CVV/CVC. It has not said how many cards or which vendors' customers are affected. Storing CVVs after authorisation is barred under PCI DSS.

deck.headline: Hackers used GL.iNet's cloud service to plant malware on routers and KVM devices
deck.summary: GL.iNet says attackers exploited a flaw in its GoodCloud remote-management service to install malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some users finding backdoors. The cloud hole is closed but infected devices stay infected. It has not said how many were hit or whether servers attached to KVMs were compromised.
deck.whyItMatters: KVM devices sit below every endpoint control; anyone who used GoodCloud to reach servers or branch machines should treat attached hosts as possibly compromised and check for the indicator.
deck.storyline: Storyline: hacks that hit the physical world · day 3
deck.detailHtml: GL.iNet makes home and travel routers and KVM-over-IP devices that let admins control servers remotely. Its GoodCloud platform manages them remotely, and the company says an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability there to install malicious software. 'The attack path has been blocked,' it says, but the fix 'does not remove malware from devices that were already infected'. It told users to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log and install the latest security firmware; it has not said how many devices were hit, and is investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were compromised. The advisory reached the Hacker News front page.

deck.headline: FBI investigates apparent crime-database hack days after White House fires its cyber chief
deck.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, the database police use for warrants and background checks. Two days earlier the White House fired cyber director Sean Cairncross after outages that hit banks and air traffic control. On Sunday a Delta system failure delayed every Delta flight at Atlanta.
deck.whyItMatters: The US government's cyber leadership is changing while a criminal-justice database may be exposed; banks that rely on NCIC-derived background checks should watch for guidance, and operational-resilience teams should expect more scrutiny after the outage run.
deck.detailHtml: US media report the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, which federal and local police use for warrants and background checks; the FBI did not comment, and Trump said he had 'just heard' about it. On 20 Nov the White House removed National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, after he lost the confidence of chief of staff Stephen Miller (CBS); Marco Rubio named Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies as successor. The removal follows last week's outages across banking, the FAA and Microsoft, which officials say were not cyberattacks. On Sunday a failure of Delta's weight-and-balance system delayed every Delta flight at Atlanta, a week after the FAA groundstop.

deck.headline: China to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing abroad unless they move home
deck.summary: China's securities regulator has told law firms it will not approve offshore listings by red-chip companies set up after 2023 unless they move their domicile to China, Reuters reports, citing sources. The unannounced guidance tightens control of capital raised abroad and could dent Hong Kong's IPO pipeline as Chinese AI stocks slump.
deck.whyItMatters: Hong Kong's IPO boom depends on mainland tech; investment banks' Asia ECM pipelines and venture exits for Chinese AI start-ups just got narrower.
deck.storyline: Storyline: China's grip on its capital markets · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Red-chip companies are registered abroad, usually in tax havens, but control businesses in China; the structure is favoured by tech start-ups listing in Hong Kong or New York. Reuters, citing people familiar, says the China Securities Regulatory Commission told law firms in recent days that red-chip companies established after the 2023 offshore-listing rules must re-domicile in China before listing offshore. The guidance is confidential and unannounced. It comes as China's AI stocks slump; the collector also carried a report that Chinese AI shares have lost about $1.7 trillion, which we could not open.

deck.headline: Drones hit Russian ships in Libya and the Gulf of Finland, sinking a corvette
deck.summary: A suspected drone attack set a Russian ship on fire at Libya's Benghazi naval base on Sunday; satellite images show a Russian corvette capsized and sunk. A day earlier drones hit the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland says Ukraine was likely behind it. Moscow has not commented.
deck.whyItMatters: The sea war is spreading to the Mediterranean and the Baltic, raising marine war-risk premiums and sanctions-enforcement questions for shipping finance.
deck.storyline: Storyline: Russian sabotage in Europe · day 3
deck.detailHtml: Libya's eastern government says an explosion at dawn on Sunday on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base, stopped for fuel on its way home, was a suspected drone attack, with no casualties; BBC Verify geolocated video of the ship in flames. US-based Vantor says images show a Project 20380 (Steregushchiy-class) corvette moored on Saturday and capsized and sunk on Sunday. A commercial vessel off Benghazi was also hit, with minor injuries. Moscow has not commented. On Saturday the US- and Ukraine-sanctioned cargo ship Sparta II, bound for Kaliningrad, was hit by two drones in the eastern Gulf of Finland, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters; Finland's defence forces say Ukraine was likely responsible. It follows Poland's report on 20 Nov of a Russian missile landing on its soil.

deck.headline: FDIC approves OneMain's industrial bank, letting it lend nationwide at up to 36%
deck.summary: OneMain has Utah and FDIC approval for OneMain Bank, an industrial loan company that must hold at least $341m of capital and a 15% leverage ratio. It will originate personal and auto loans and cards through 1,300 storefronts, offer one product nationwide at up to 36% APR, and take its BrightWay card in-house from WebBank.
deck.whyItMatters: It continues the fintech-charter wave (OakNorth, Payoneer, MoonPay this month); sponsor banks such as WebBank lose programmes, and consumer-lending competition at the 36% ceiling grows.
deck.detailHtml: Twenty months after applying, OneMain has approval from Utah's Department of Financial Institutions and deposit insurance from the FDIC for OneMain Bank, an industrial loan company. Per the FDIC order, it must raise at least $341m of paid-in capital and keep a 15% leverage ratio; as an ILC owner OneMain avoids becoming a bank holding company but signs a parent company agreement giving the FDIC oversight. The bank will originate unsecured and auto loans and credit cards, funded mainly by brokered deposits, and sell most of them to OneMain, which will distribute them through 1,300+ storefronts in 44 states. The charter lets it replace state-by-state licensing with a single product nationwide at up to 36% APR, and issue its BrightWay card itself instead of through WebBank. It expects to be operating in about a year. Fintech Business Weekly asks whether Dave can follow where Enova and OppFi did not.

alsoToday.headline: AI agent builders ace their own tests but barely improve on hidden cases

alsoToday.headline: Builders point volunteer AI agent fleets at P vs NP, with Lean checking every step

alsoToday.headline: Google previews checks that block an AI agent's tool call before it runs
alsoToday.summary: The check sits outside the agent. A language model compares each proposed tool call with the user's request and written policies, so an agent talked out of its instructions by a user or a poisoned document is still stopped at the gateway.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: This is the control pattern regulators will expect for agentic banking: policy enforced outside the model, at the action.
